children: By Joe Light

President Donald Trump's promise to pay every American adult $5,000 if Republicans win the midterm elections not only has daunting political challenges, but economic ones, too-as much as $1.4 trillion added to the national debt and quite possibly a spike in inflation.
The forecasts come from budget modeler Kent Smetters, though an exact estimate is tough because of lots of variables.

Trump made the pledge Wednesday in a two-hour speech at the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas, telling the crowd that "the Trump dividend" would come if Republicans retain control of both the House and the Senate. Later in the evening, Vice President JD Vance said the checks wouldn't go to the wealthy.
On Thursday, the White House didn't provide details of the plan.

"President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong, drawing a clear contrast with the Democrats' record of historic inflation, unfettered illegal immigration, skyrocketing crime, and weakness on the world stage," said spokesman Davis Ingle in a statement.

Whether the $5,000 goes to every American adult or to only those below an income cap, the national debt would still increase by at least $1 trillion, according to Smetters, who is faculty director of the Penn Wharton Budget Model.
Today, the government owes more than $40 trillion-a record amount and growing.

Based on the president's pledge of a check for every adult American, the package would cost about $1.35 trillion, Smetters said. If the $5,000 checks had a household income cap of $400,000, the plan would cost $1.15 trillion, Smetters said.
Then, there's the matter of the annual inflation rate, which stood at 3.4% in July; the August number is due out on Friday.

If recipients spend only about $400 billion in the six months after receiving the money-roughly 30% of the $1.35 trillion-inflation would increase as much as half of a percentage point over the following year, Smetters said.
Plus, he said, the increase in the federal deficit-the amount that spending exceeds revenue in a year-would cause interest rates to rise.
The magnitude of the increase, though, is impossible to estimate without knowing how the Federal Reserve and Treasury Department would change their own bond-buying programs in response.
Today, the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate is 6.76%, according to Freddie Mac.

A calculator created by the Yale Budget Lab estimates that a one-time $1.15 trillion debt increase would add about 0.07 of a percentage point to a fixed 30-year rate. For a $250,000 mortgage, that would add to an extra $139 a year.

Mortgage rates are tied to the 10-year Treasury yield, which rose 0.09 of a percentage point on Thursday. So far, bond investors seem skeptical that Trump's plan has even a remote chance of happening.

Debt hawks have fared poorly this year in primary elections, dampening the political will to shrink the deficit. But a plan to increase the deficit by more than $1 trillion, even if just for a year, almost certainly won't get much support even from the president's fellow Republicans.
Trump has made promises of checks before-ones tied to savings from cuts by the so-called Department of Government Efficiency or tariff revenue. Congress never followed through.

With full control of the House and the Senate, Republicans could try to move forward with Trump's midterm dividend plan right now instead of waiting for the election. That they aren't speaks to the idea's lack of political support.
